`type: artifact-typedef`, `id`, `defines` (the type name instances carry

2. **Required frontmatter** — the instance field set, closed unless

3. **Required sections** — the instance body structure.
4. **Commitment (Definition of Done)** — when an instance is done, with a

5. **Sources** — the established forms the type composes; format

An artifact-typedef is done when a validator can check any instance from
it alone and an author can write a conforming instance from its rendered
template alone. **Consequence on failure:** instances of the type cannot
be validated, so none are deliverable.

ISO/IEC/IEEE 15289 (generic content types); DITA specialization and
ancestry declaration; Scrum's artifact-commitment pairing; the live

# Base writing style

These rules apply to everything written for a human reader, regardless of
document type. Document types add a format layer on top of this base; they
never override it.

## Goal

The reader gets the point of any paragraph in one read, any section in 30
seconds, and the whole document in two minutes. Write for the first read.

## Lead with the point

At every scale, state the conclusion first and the support after.

- A document opens with what it found or decided, not how it got there.
- A section opens with its main claim, then evidence.
- A paragraph opens with its point, then elaboration.

If a document type defines a structure, that structure is just this rule
applied to that type. If no structure is defined, use this rule to invent
one.

## Detail placement

Precision serves the point; it never precedes it. Formal specification
language, methods, raw data, scoring tables, and citations go after the
claim they support — or in an appendix. The body is for understanding.

## Sentences

- One idea per sentence.
- Active voice, with a named actor: "Reviewers delete unlinked checks,"
  not "Unlinked checks are subject to deletion."
- Prefer the short common word: "use" not "utilize," "end" not
  "terminate," "before" not "prior to."

## Terminology

- Never use a metaphor as a technical term. If a word describes a thing
  by what it resembles instead of what it literally does, replace it with
  the literal description. Test: could a competent reader from outside
  the team work out the meaning from the words alone? If not, rewrite.
- Banned words. Never use these, in any form:
  - "load-bearing" → say "other work depends on it" or "critical to
    operations"
  - "surface" (as in context surface, config surface) → say "input,"
    "source," or "channel"
  - "seam" → say "boundary" or "integration point"
  - "scar tissue" → describe the actual problem, e.g. "an unreviewed
    workaround that was never removed"
- Explain every insider reference — a past incident, an internal system,
  a person — in one plain sentence, or cut it. Assume the reader knows
  none of our history.

## Style examples

These examples exist only to show sentence style. The domain (a public
library) is deliberately unrelated to our work. Copy the style; never
copy the content or vocabulary into real documents.

bad:

> Unreturned inventory constitutes scar tissue on the circulation loop
> and rapidly becomes load-bearing for downstream shelving throughput.

good:

> Overdue books pile up at the front desk, and staff spend their time
> reshelving late returns instead of helping visitors.

The bad sentence uses two metaphors as terms and never names an actor.
The good sentence says who is affected and what actually happens, in
plain words.

# Experience principles

## What this set governs

This is the experience-scope principle set: the standing rules for how
the product's interactions are designed, whichever interaction type a
person or an agent reaches the product by — command line, terminal,
graphical or web, API and SDK, conversational, voice, or a generated
document. It is a peer of the working-scope set,
[Founding principles](principles.md), which governs how every activity
is performed, and of the architecture-scope set,
[Architecture principles](architecture-principles.md), which governs
what the designed system must look like; this set governs what a person
or an agent meets when they use it. It is the first layer of the
experience guidance corpus the
[product designer role](roles/lead-product-designer.md) owns; the
guidelines that apply it to each interaction type sit beneath it.
Backticked slugs cite principles; a slug not defined in this document is
defined in the working or architecture set. The terms interaction type,
experience guidance corpus, generated interface, BC-shop, contract, and
intent are defined in the [glossary](glossary.md). Two words carry one
sense each here: an *agent* is a software caller using the product on
someone's behalf; an *assistant interaction* is one in which the
product itself acts on an intent the person stated rather than on a
command — conversational, voice, or an assistant acting for the person
(a closed set; the solutions architect role is the lead shop's
architecture role). Where a principle here applies another set's
principle at the experience level, the frontmatter declares the lineage
in `derives-from` instead of restating the rule as a second authority.

## What a good principle looks like

This section restates the shared definition from the
[principle-set typedef](artifacts/principle-set.md) so this document can
be read alone; the restatement is a rendering, not a second authority.

A principle is a standing rule, in four parts: a name, a statement, a
rationale, and implications.

- The **statement** is the rule. It carries the only normative keywords
  (MUST, SHOULD, MAY — interpreted per BCP 14 when, and only when, they
  appear in capitals) and is testable: shown a piece of work, you can
  answer yes or no. A statement carrying more than one obligation
  presents one obligation per bullet.
- The **rationale** says why the rule earns its place: the failure it
  prevents, shown as a generic example; well-known external references
  may support it, the product's own history never appears. Rationales
  stay prose.
- The **implications** are the price tag: one implication per bullet,
  the concrete change each named actor absorbs to honor the rule. They
  add no obligations — every implication must be derivable from the
  statement.

A good principle passes the tests applied in the fitness screen at the
end: its statement is testable (TOGAF's understandable, complete,
consistent); it helps you say no (Jared Spool, "Creating Great Design
Principles"); it is not fluff and not a goal in disguise (Richard
Rumelt, *Good Strategy/Bad Strategy*); it is not permission-to-play —
something every competent product already does (Patrick Lencioni, "Make
Your Values Mean Something"); and it implies at least one practice and
at least one check.

## The principles

### Consistent, not uniform (`consistent-not-uniform`)

**Statement.**
- Every interaction type MUST name the product's things and actions with
  the product's one vocabulary, as the experience guidance corpus
  records it.
- Every interaction type MUST follow, for its form and idiom, the
  platform interface guidelines the corpus names for that type.
- Where a platform guideline names an action differently from the
  vocabulary, the platform's word MUST be used in that interaction
  type and the mapping recorded in the vocabulary.
- A rule of the corpus MAY be varied for one interaction type only
  with the variation and its reason recorded in the corpus.

**Rationale.** A product reached through a command line, a web page,
and a chat window is three products when each names the same object
differently, and a foreign one when its command line ignores the
terminal's conventions to imitate its web page. People carry their
expectations from the platform they are on — Nielsen Norman Group's
usability heuristic "consistency and standards" and Jakob's law of
internet user experience — and from the last place they met the
product. The GOV.UK design principles put it as "be consistent, not
uniform": the same language and patterns wherever possible, without a
straitjacket. Words and rules are shared; form follows the platform.

**Implications.**
- The product designer role maintains the vocabulary, its per-platform
  mappings, and the named platform guidelines per interaction type in
  the corpus.
- The product designer role screens every interaction type's text
  against the vocabulary.
- BC-shops building an interaction cite the platform guideline the
  corpus names for its type.
- The product designer role records each variation with its reason; an
  unrecorded variation is a finding against the corpus.

### Core-task parity (`core-task-parity`)

**Statement.**
- Every interaction type the product offers MUST support every task on
  the corpus's core-task list.
- An option the product offers in one interaction type MUST be
  reachable in every other interaction type that presents the same
  task.

**Rationale.** A voice assistant that can start an order but only a
screen can confirm it strands the person who has no screen; a chat
interface that offers three choices only one of which the graphical
interface shows teaches people that the product hides things. Google's
conversation design guidelines and Amazon's Alexa design guide converge
on the rule: voice-first but not voice-only, every option offered in
one modality reachable in the other, the core message the same across
them. Parity of tasks and options is what lets a person move between
interaction types without relearning what the product can do.

**Implications.**
- The product designer role keeps the core-task list in the corpus.
- The product designer role screens each new interaction type against
  the list before delivery.
- BC-shops that add an option to one interaction type add it to every
  other type presenting that task.
- The PO role's acceptance scenarios for a task name the interaction
  types it must hold on.

### The agent is a user (`agent-is-a-user`)

**Statement.**
- Every interface an agent uses to reach the product — a tool
  definition, a command line, an API, or an SDK (a closed set) — MUST
  be designed as an interface: named for its caller, its behavior
  stated in its documentation, and screened by the product designer
  role.
- An agent-facing interface MUST NOT expose a capability a person could
  not reach through some interaction type.

**Rationale.** A tool whose parameters are named for the implementer
rather than the caller is misread by the agent calling it, and the
agent's failure is recorded as the agent's. Nielsen Norman Group's "AI
Agents as Users" states the shift plainly — "user" is no longer
synonymous with "human" — and Anthropic's guidance on building agents
asks for as much care in the agent-computer interface as in the human
one. This principle is `actor-neutral-discipline` applied at the
interface: the discipline of design does not lapse because the user is
an agent, and an agent gains no capability a person lacks. An interface
no one designed is still an interface; it is only an undesigned one.

**Implications.**
- The solutions architect role submits contracts, command lines, and
  tool definitions to the product designer role's screen before they
  are published.
- BC-shops write tool and API documentation for the caller, with the
  same care as user-facing help.
- The product designer role screens agent-facing interfaces against
  the corpus with the same patterns as human-facing ones.

### Evidence, not opinion (`evidence-not-opinion`)

**Statement.**
- A claim that an interaction is usable MUST rest on observed use — a
  user test, a tested prototype, or measured task completion (a closed
  set the corpus may extend) — or be labeled a hypothesis.
- A preference — a stakeholder's, a maker's, the designer's own — MUST
  NOT decide a design question that observed use can answer; what the
  product is for is the PM role's decision, not a design question.

**Rationale.** Design by committee, where every opinion in the room
weighs the same, produces the least-common-denominator interface; the
alternative is not one taste in charge but one decision-maker deciding
on evidence. Human-centred design as ISO 9241-210 describes it is
driven and refined by user-centred evaluation; GOV.UK's third design
principle is "design with data." Nielsen Norman Group's "The
Product-Manager Archetype" names the failure the second bullet
prevents: a sketch handed over as a requirement, with the designer
asked to polish it instead of to test it.

**Implications.**
- The product designer role records the evidence behind each design
  decision in the corpus, and labels the rest hypotheses.
- The PM role treats a wireframe or sketch from any role as input to be
  tested, never as a requirement.
- BC-shops label an untested interaction's usability a hypothesis when
  they deliver it.

### Accessible by standard (`accessible-by-standard`)

**Statement.**
- Every graphical, web, and document interaction MUST meet WCAG 2.2 at
  level AA.
- Every non-web interaction — command line, terminal, voice, and
  assistant interactions (a closed set; APIs and SDKs are agent-facing
  and governed by `agent-is-a-user`) — MUST apply the WCAG 2.2
  success criteria as WCAG2ICT describes for non-web software, with a
  record of which criteria do not apply and why.
- Accessibility conformance MUST be established before an interaction
  is delivered.

**Rationale.** An interface that conveys meaning by color alone, or a
terminal screen that a screen reader cannot follow, excludes the people
who depend on assistive technology and, increasingly, the agents that
read the same structure. The W3C's guidelines are the one shared
standard — WCAG 2.2 is ISO/IEC 40500:2025 — and, as GOV.UK's sixth
design principle has it, accessible design is good design: the
discipline it imposes, clear names and predictable structure, serves
every user. Retrofitting accessibility costs more than building it and
reaches fewer.

**Implications.**
- The product designer role names the accessibility target per
  interaction type in the corpus, with the WCAG2ICT applicability
  record for non-web types.
- BC-shops test each interaction with assistive technology before
  delivery and attach the result.
- The PO role's acceptance scenarios for an interaction include its
  accessibility criteria.

### Errors guide recovery (`errors-guide-recovery`)

**Statement.**
- Every error the product shows MUST say what happened, in the
  product's vocabulary and the person's natural language, and what the
  person can do next.
- An error MUST NOT expose an internal identifier or message in place
  of that explanation, though it MAY carry one alongside it.

**Rationale.** A command that fails with a stack trace, a form that
says "invalid input" without saying which field, a chat assistant that
answers a misunderstanding with silence — each leaves the person to
guess, and in a command line, where there is no interface to guide
them, the error message is the interface. The Command Line Interface
Guidelines (clig.dev) say it directly: catch errors and rewrite them
for humans. Microsoft's Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction ask the
same of assistants — support efficient correction — and Google's
conversation design guidelines warn that one poorly handled error
outweighs dozens of successful turns.

**Implications.**
- BC-shops write every user-facing error with its next step, and keep
  the internal detail in a log or an alongside field.
- The product designer role screens error text against the vocabulary
  and voice.
- The solutions architect role's contracts define error responses that
  carry a human-readable explanation, not only a code.

### Control stays with the person (`control-stays-with-the-person`)

**Statement.**
- An assistant interaction MUST make clear what the product can do.
- An assistant interaction MUST say what it is about to do before an
  action the corpus classes as hard to reverse.
- An assistant interaction MUST let the person correct, dismiss, or
  stop it at any point.
- An assistant interaction MUST hand control back to the person when it
  fails.
- A generated interface MUST stay within the constraints the corpus
  states for it; it MAY vary its form within them.

**Rationale.** Intent-based interaction reverses the locus of control:
the person states an outcome and the system chooses the steps. That is
its value and its danger. An assistant that books the wrong thing
silently, or cannot be interrupted, or shows a different interface each
visit, loses the trust that makes delegation possible. Microsoft's
Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction — make clear what the system can
do, support efficient invocation, dismissal, and correction, provide
global controls — and Ben Shneiderman's *Human-Centered AI*, which
holds that high automation and high human control are compatible
rather than a trade-off, point the same way: the system may act, and
the person stays in charge.

**Implications.**
- BC-shops building an assistant interaction implement the confirm,
  correct, dismiss, and stop controls before the interaction is
  delivered.
- The product designer role screens assistant interactions against the
  human-AI guidelines named in the corpus.
- The product designer role states, in the corpus, which actions are
  hard to reverse and the constraints a generated interface varies
  within.

## Fitness screen (the intro's tests; sources: TOGAF, Spool, Rumelt, Lencioni)

| Screen | consistent-not-uniform | core-task-parity | agent-is-a-user | evidence-not-opinion | accessible-by-standard | errors-guide-recovery | control-stays-with-the-person |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Statement testable (TOGAF: understandable, complete, consistent) | pass — precedence stated between vocabulary and platform | pass — against the corpus's list | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass |
| Helps you say no (Spool) | yes: rejects a second name for one thing and a CLI that imitates a web page | yes: rejects a task or option offered on one type only | yes: rejects an undesigned tool definition and an agent-only capability | yes: rejects a preference deciding a testable question | yes: rejects color-only meaning and accessibility as a later pass | yes: rejects a bare code or stack trace as an error | yes: rejects silent action, uninterruptible assistants, and unconstrained generated interfaces |
| Not fluff, not a goal-in-disguise (Rumelt) | pass — directs without prescribing form | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass |
| Not permission-to-play (Lencioni) | pass — most multi-interface products drift into several vocabularies | pass — most voice and chat interfaces are subsets of the screen | pass — most tool definitions are named for the implementer | pass — most design questions are settled by the loudest preference | pass on bullets 2 and 3 —

# Base writing style

These rules apply to everything written for a human reader, regardless of
document type. Document types add a format layer on top of this base; they
never override it.

## Goal

The reader gets the point of any paragraph in one read, any section in 30
seconds, and the whole document in two minutes. Write for the first read.

## Lead with the point

At every scale, state the conclusion first and the support after.

- A document opens with what it found or decided, not how it got there.
- A section opens with its main claim, then evidence.
- A paragraph opens with its point, then elaboration.

If a document type defines a structure, that structure is just this rule
applied to that type. If no structure is defined, use this rule to invent
one.

## Detail placement

Precision serves the point; it never precedes it. Formal specification
language, methods, raw data, scoring tables, and citations go after the
claim they support — or in an appendix. The body is for understanding.

## Sentences

- One idea per sentence.
- Active voice, with a named actor: "Reviewers delete unlinked checks,"
  not "Unlinked checks are subject to deletion."
- Prefer the short common word: "use" not "utilize," "end" not
  "terminate," "before" not "prior to."

## Terminology

- Never use a metaphor as a technical term. If a word describes a thing
  by what it resembles instead of what it literally does, replace it with
  the literal description. Test: could a competent reader from outside
  the team work out the meaning from the words alone? If not, rewrite.
- Banned words. Never use these, in any form:
  - "load-bearing" → say "other work depends on it" or "critical to
    operations"
  - "surface" (as in context surface, config surface) → say "input,"
    "source," or "channel"
  - "seam" → say "boundary" or "integration point"
  - "scar tissue" → describe the actual problem, e.g. "an unreviewed
    workaround that was never removed"
- Explain every insider reference — a past incident, an internal system,
  a person — in one plain sentence, or cut it. Assume the reader knows
  none of our history.

## Style examples

These examples exist only to show sentence style. The domain (a public
library) is deliberately unrelated to our work. Copy the style; never
copy the content or vocabulary into real documents.

bad:

> Unreturned inventory constitutes scar tissue on the circulation loop
> and rapidly becomes load-bearing for downstream shelving throughput.

good:

> Overdue books pile up at the front desk, and staff spend their time
> reshelving late returns instead of helping visitors.

The bad sentence uses two metaphors as terms and never names an actor.
The good sentence says who is affected and what actually happens, in
plain words.

# Experience principles

## What this set governs

This is the experience-scope principle set: the standing rules for how
the product's interactions are designed, whichever interaction type a
person or an agent reaches the product by — command line, terminal,
graphical or web, API and SDK, conversational, voice, or a generated
document. It is a peer of the working-scope set,
[Founding principles](principles.md), which governs how every activity
is performed, and of the architecture-scope set,
[Architecture principles](architecture-principles.md), which governs
what the designed system must look like; this set governs what a person
or an agent meets when they use it. It is the first layer of the
experience guidance corpus the
[product designer role](roles/lead-product-designer.md) owns; the
guidelines that apply it to each interaction type sit beneath it.
Backticked slugs cite principles; a slug not defined in this document is
defined in the working or architecture set. The terms interaction type,
experience guidance corpus, generated interface, BC-shop, contract, and
intent are defined in the [glossary](glossary.md). Two words carry one
sense each here: an *agent* is a software caller using the product on
someone's behalf; an *assistant interaction* is one in which the
product itself acts on an intent the person stated rather than on a
command — conversational, voice, or an assistant acting for the person
(a closed set; the solutions architect role is the lead shop's
architecture role). Where a principle here applies another set's
principle at the experience level, the frontmatter declares the lineage
in `derives-from` instead of restating the rule as a second authority.

## What a good principle looks like

This section restates the shared definition from the
[principle-set typedef](artifacts/principle-set.md) so this document can
be read alone; the restatement is a rendering, not a second authority.

A principle is a standing rule, in four parts: a name, a statement, a
rationale, and implications.

- The **statement** is the rule. It carries the only normative keywords
  (MUST, SHOULD, MAY — interpreted per BCP 14 when, and only when, they
  appear in capitals) and is testable: shown a piece of work, you can
  answer yes or no. A statement carrying more than one obligation
  presents one obligation per bullet.
- The **rationale** says why the rule earns its place: the failure it
  prevents, shown as a generic example; well-known external references
  may support it, the product's own history never appears. Rationales
  stay prose.
- The **implications** are the price tag: one implication per bullet,
  the concrete change each named actor absorbs to honor the rule. They
  add no obligations — every implication must be derivable from the
  statement.

A good principle passes the tests applied in the fitness screen at the
end: its statement is testable (TOGAF's understandable, complete,
consistent); it helps you say no (Jared Spool, "Creating Great Design
Principles"); it is not fluff and not a goal in disguise (Richard
Rumelt, *Good Strategy/Bad Strategy*); it is not permission-to-play —
something every competent product already does (Patrick Lencioni, "Make
Your Values Mean Something"); and it implies at least one practice and
at least one check.

## The principles

### Consistent, not uniform (`consistent-not-uniform`)

**Statement.**
- Every interaction type MUST name the product's things and actions with
  the product's one vocabulary, as the experience guidance corpus
  records it.
- Every interaction type MUST follow, for its form and idiom, the
  platform interface guidelines the corpus names for that type.
- Where a platform guideline names an action differently from the
  vocabulary, the platform's word MUST be used in that interaction
  type and the mapping recorded in the vocabulary.
- A rule of the corpus MAY be varied for one interaction type only
  with the variation and its reason recorded in the corpus.

**Rationale.** A product reached through a command line, a web page,
and a chat window is three products when each names the same object
differently, and a foreign one when its command line ignores the
terminal's conventions to imitate its web page. People carry their
expectations from the platform they are on — Nielsen Norman Group's
usability heuristic "consistency and standards" and Jakob's law of
internet user experience — and from the last place they met the
product. The GOV.UK design principles put it as "be consistent, not
uniform": the same language and patterns wherever possible, without a
straitjacket. Words and rules are shared; form follows the platform.

**Implications.**
- The product designer role maintains the vocabulary, its per-platform
  mappings, and the named platform guidelines per interaction type in
  the corpus.
- The product designer role screens every interaction type's text
  against the vocabulary.
- BC-shops building an interaction cite the platform guideline the
  corpus names for its type.
- The product designer role records each variation with its reason; an
  unrecorded variation is a finding against the corpus.

### Core-task parity (`core-task-parity`)

**Statement.**
- Every interaction type the product offers MUST support every task on
  the corpus's core-task list.
- An option the product offers in one interaction type MUST be
  reachable in every other interaction type that presents the same
  task.

**Rationale.** A voice assistant that can start an order but only a
screen can confirm it strands the person who has no screen; a chat
interface that offers three choices only one of which the graphical
interface shows teaches people that the product hides things. Google's
conversation design guidelines and Amazon's Alexa design guide converge
on the rule: voice-first but not voice-only, every option offered in
one modality reachable in the other, the core message the same across
them. Parity of tasks and options is what lets a person move between
interaction types without relearning what the product can do.

**Implications.**
- The product designer role keeps the core-task list in the corpus.
- The product designer role screens each new interaction type against
  the list before delivery.
- BC-shops that add an option to one interaction type add it to every
  other type presenting that task.
- The PO role's acceptance scenarios for a task name the interaction
  types it must hold on.

### The agent is a user (`agent-is-a-user`)

**Statement.**
- Every interface an agent uses to reach the product — a tool
  definition, a command line, an API, or an SDK (a closed set) — MUST
  be designed as an interface: named for its caller, its behavior
  stated in its documentation, and screened by the product designer
  role.
- An agent-facing interface MUST NOT expose a capability a person could
  not reach through some interaction type.

**Rationale.** A tool whose parameters are named for the implementer
rather than the caller is misread by the agent calling it, and the
agent's failure is recorded as the agent's. Nielsen Norman Group's "AI
Agents as Users" states the shift plainly — "user" is no longer
synonymous with "human" — and Anthropic's guidance on building agents
asks for as much care in the agent-computer interface as in the human
one. This principle is `actor-neutral-discipline` applied at the
interface: the discipline of design does not lapse because the user is
an agent, and an agent gains no capability a person lacks. An interface
no one designed is still an interface; it is only an undesigned one.

**Implications.**
- The solutions architect role submits contracts, command lines, and
  tool definitions to the product designer role's screen before they
  are published.
- BC-shops write tool and API documentation for the caller, with the
  same care as user-facing help.
- The product designer role screens agent-facing interfaces against
  the corpus with the same patterns as human-facing ones.

### Evidence, not opinion (`evidence-not-opinion`)

**Statement.**
- A claim that an interaction is usable MUST rest on observed use — a
  user test, a tested prototype, or measured task completion (a closed
  set the corpus may extend) — or be labeled a hypothesis.
- A preference — a stakeholder's, a maker's, the designer's own — MUST
  NOT decide a design question that observed use can answer; what the
  product is for is the PM role's decision, not a design question.

**Rationale.** Design by committee, where every opinion in the room
weighs the same, produces the least-common-denominator interface; the
alternative is not one taste in charge but one decision-maker deciding
on evidence. Human-centred design as ISO 9241-210 describes it is
driven and refined by user-centred evaluation; GOV.UK's third design
principle is "design with data." Nielsen Norman Group's "The
Product-Manager Archetype" names the failure the second bullet
prevents: a sketch handed over as a requirement, with the designer
asked to polish it instead of to test it.

**Implications.**
- The product designer role records the evidence behind each design
  decision in the corpus, and labels the rest hypotheses.
- The PM role treats a wireframe or sketch from any role as input to be
  tested, never as a requirement.
- BC-shops label an untested interaction's usability a hypothesis when
  they deliver it.

### Accessible by standard (`accessible-by-standard`)

**Statement.**
- Every graphical, web, and document interaction MUST meet WCAG 2.2 at
  level AA.
- Every non-web interaction — command line, terminal, voice, and
  assistant interactions (a closed set; APIs and SDKs are agent-facing
  and governed by `agent-is-a-user`) — MUST apply the WCAG 2.2
  success criteria as WCAG2ICT describes for non-web software, with a
  record of which criteria do not apply and why.
- Accessibility conformance MUST be established before an interaction
  is delivered.

**Rationale.** An interface that conveys meaning by color alone, or a
terminal screen that a screen reader cannot follow, excludes the people
who depend on assistive technology and, increasingly, the agents that
read the same structure. The W3C's guidelines are the one shared
standard — WCAG 2.2 is ISO/IEC 40500:2025 — and, as GOV.UK's sixth
design principle has it, accessible design is good design: the
discipline it imposes, clear names and predictable structure, serves
every user. Retrofitting accessibility costs more than building it and
reaches fewer.

**Implications.**
- The product designer role names the accessibility target per
  interaction type in the corpus, with the WCAG2ICT applicability
  record for non-web types.
- BC-shops test each interaction with assistive technology before
  delivery and attach the result.
- The PO role's acceptance scenarios for an interaction include its
  accessibility criteria.

### Errors guide recovery (`errors-guide-recovery`)

**Statement.**
- Every error the product shows MUST say what happened, in the
  product's vocabulary and the person's natural language, and what the
  person can do next.
- An error MUST NOT expose an internal identifier or message in place
  of that explanation, though it MAY carry one alongside it.

**Rationale.** A command that fails with a stack trace, a form that
says "invalid input" without saying which field, a chat assistant that
answers a misunderstanding with silence — each leaves the person to
guess, and in a command line, where there is no interface to guide
them, the error message is the interface. The Command Line Interface
Guidelines (clig.dev) say it directly: catch errors and rewrite them
for humans. Microsoft's Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction ask the
same of assistants — support efficient correction — and Google's
conversation design guidelines warn that one poorly handled error
outweighs dozens of successful turns.

**Implications.**
- BC-shops write every user-facing error with its next step, and keep
  the internal detail in a log or an alongside field.
- The product designer role screens error text against the vocabulary
  and voice.
- The solutions architect role's contracts define error responses that
  carry a human-readable explanation, not only a code.

### Control stays with the person (`control-stays-with-the-person`)

**Statement.**
- An assistant interaction MUST make clear what the product can do.
- An assistant interaction MUST say what it is about to do before an
  action the corpus classes as hard to reverse.
- An assistant interaction MUST let the person correct, dismiss, or
  stop it at any point.
- An assistant interaction MUST hand control back to the person when it
  fails.
- A generated interface MUST stay within the constraints the corpus
  states for it; it MAY vary its form within them.

**Rationale.** Intent-based interaction reverses the locus of control:
the person states an outcome and the system chooses the steps. That is
its value and its danger. An assistant that books the wrong thing
silently, or cannot be interrupted, or shows a different interface each
visit, loses the trust that makes delegation possible. Microsoft's
Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction — make clear what the system can
do, support efficient invocation, dismissal, and correction, provide
global controls — and Ben Shneiderman's *Human-Centered AI*, which
holds that high automation and high human control are compatible
rather than a trade-off, point the same way: the system may act, and
the person stays in charge.

**Implications.**
- BC-shops building an assistant interaction implement the confirm,
  correct, dismiss, and stop controls before the interaction is
  delivered.
- The product designer role screens assistant interactions against the
  human-AI guidelines named in the corpus.
- The product designer role states, in the corpus, which actions are
  hard to reverse and the constraints a generated interface varies
  within.

## Fitness screen (the intro's tests; sources: TOGAF, Spool, Rumelt, Lencioni)

| Screen | consistent-not-uniform | core-task-parity | agent-is-a-user | evidence-not-opinion | accessible-by-standard | errors-guide-recovery | control-stays-with-the-person |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Statement testable (TOGAF: understandable, complete, consistent) | pass — precedence stated between vocabulary and platform | pass — against the corpus's list | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass |
| Helps you say no (Spool) | yes: rejects a second name for one thing and a CLI that imitates a web page | yes: rejects a task or option offered on one type only | yes: rejects an undesigned tool definition and an agent-only capability | yes: rejects a preference deciding a testable question | yes: rejects color-only meaning and accessibility as a later pass | yes: rejects a bare code or stack trace as an error | yes: rejects silent action, uninterruptible assistants, and unconstrained generated interfaces |
| Not fluff, not a goal-in-disguise (Rumelt) | pass — directs without prescribing form | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass |
| Not permission-to-play (Lencioni) | pass — most multi-interface products drift into several vocabularies | pass — most voice and chat interfaces are subsets of the screen | pass — most tool definitions are named for the implementer | pass — most design questions are settled by the loudest preference | pass on bullets 2 and 3 —

13	
14	These rules apply to everything written for a human reader, regardless of
15	document type. Document types add a format layer on top of this base; they
16	never override it.
17	
18	## Goal
19	
20	The reader gets the point of any paragraph in one read, any section in 30
21	seconds, and the whole document in two minutes. Write for the first read.
22	
23	## Lead with the point
24	
25	At every scale, state the conclusion first and the support after.
26	
27	- A document opens with what it found or decided, not how it got there.
28	- A section opens with its main claim, then evidence.
29	- A paragraph opens with its point, then elaboration.
30	
31	If a document type defines a structure, that structure is just this rule
32	applied to that type. If no structure is defined, use this rule to invent
33	one.

35	## Detail placement
36	
37	Precision serves the point; it never precedes it. Formal specification
38	language, methods, raw data, scoring tables, and citations go after the
39	claim they support — or in an appendix. The body is for understanding.

43	- One idea per sentence.

# Base writing style

These rules apply to everything written for a human reader, regardless of
document type. Document types add a format layer on top of this base; they
never override it.

## Goal

The reader gets the point of any paragraph in one read, any section in 30
seconds, and the whole document in two minutes. Write for the first read.

## Lead with the point

At every scale, state the conclusion first and the support after.

- A document opens with what it found or decided, not how it got there.
- A section opens with its main claim, then evidence.
- A paragraph opens with its point, then elaboration.

If a document type defines a structure, that structure is just this rule
applied to that type. If no structure is defined, use this rule to invent
one.

## Detail placement

Precision serves the point; it never precedes it. Formal specification
language, methods, raw data, scoring tables, and citations go after the
claim they support — or in an appendix. The body is for understanding.

## Sentences

- One idea per sentence.
- Active voice, with a named actor: "Reviewers delete unlinked checks,"
  not "Unlinked checks are subject to deletion."
- Prefer the short common word: "use" not "utilize," "end" not
  "terminate," "before" not "prior to."

## Terminology

- Never use a metaphor as a technical term. If a word describes a thing
  by what it resembles instead of what it literally does, replace it with
  the literal description. Test: could a competent reader from outside
  the team work out the meaning from the words alone? If not, rewrite.
- Banned words. Never use these, in any form:
  - "load-bearing" → say "other work depends on it" or "critical to
    operations"
  - "surface" (as in context surface, config surface) → say "input,"
    "source," or "channel"
  - "seam" → say "boundary" or "integration point"
  - "scar tissue" → describe the actual problem, e.g. "an unreviewed
    workaround that was never removed"
- Explain every insider reference — a past incident, an internal system,
  a person — in one plain sentence, or cut it. Assume the reader knows
  none of our history.

## Style examples

These examples exist only to show sentence style. The domain (a public
library) is deliberately unrelated to our work. Copy the style; never
copy the content or vocabulary into real documents.

bad:

> Unreturned inventory constitutes scar tissue on the circulation loop
> and rapidly becomes load-bearing for downstream shelving throughput.

good:

> Overdue books pile up at the front desk, and staff spend their time
> reshelving late returns instead of helping visitors.

The bad sentence uses two metaphors as terms and never names an actor.
The good sentence says who is affected and what actually happens, in
plain words.

3	id: experience-principles
4	scope: experience
5	owner: product-authority

12	  agent-is-a-user: actor-neutral-discipline
13	---
14	
15	# Experience principles
16	
17	## What this set governs
18	
19	This is the experience-scope principle set: the standing rules for how
20	the product's interactions are designed, whichever interaction type a
21	person or an agent reaches the product by — command line, terminal,
22	graphical or web, API and SDK, conversational, voice, or a generated
23	document. It is a peer of the working-scope set,
24	[Founding principles](principles.md), which governs how every activity
25	is performed, and of the architecture-scope set,
26	[Architecture principles](architecture-principles.md), which governs
27	what the designed system must look like; this set governs what a person
28	or an agent meets when they use it. It is the first layer of the
29	experience guidance corpus the
30	[product designer role](roles/lead-product-designer.md) owns; the
31	guidelines that apply it to each interaction type sit beneath it.
32	Backticked slugs cite principles; a slug not defined in this document is
33	defined in the working or architecture set. The terms interaction type,
34	experience guidance corpus, generated interface, BC-shop, contract, and
35	intent are defined in the [glossary](glossary.md). Two words carry one
36	sense each here: an *agent* is a software caller using the product on
37	someone's behalf; an *assistant interaction* is one in which the
38	product itself acts on an intent the person stated rather than on a
39	command — conversational, voice, or an assistant acting for the person
40	(a closed set; the solutions architect role is the lead shop's
41	architecture role). Where a principle here applies another set's
42	principle at the experience level, the frontmatter declares the lineage
43	in `derives-from` instead of restating the rule as a second authority.
44	
45	## What a good principle looks like
46	
47	This section restates the shared definition from the
48	[principle-set typedef](artifacts/principle-set.md) so this document can
49	be read alone; the restatement is a rendering, not a second authority.
50	
51	A principle is a standing rule, in four parts: a name, a statement, a
52	rationale, and implications.
53	
54	- The **statement** is the rule. It carries the only normative keywords
55	  (MUST, SHOULD, MAY — interpreted per BCP 14 when, and only when, they
56	  appear in capitals) and is testable: shown a piece of work, you can
57	  answer yes or no. A statement carrying more than one obligation
58	  presents one obligation per bullet.
59	- The **rationale** says why the rule earns its place: the failure it
60	  prevents, shown as a generic example; well-known external references
61	  may support it, the product's own history never appears. Rationales
62	  stay prose.
63	- The **implications** are the price tag: one implication per bullet,
64	  the concrete change each named actor absorbs to honor the rule. They
65	  add no obligations — every implication must be derivable from the
66	  statement.
67	
68	A good principle passes the tests applied in the fitness screen at the
69	end: its statement is testable (TOGAF's understandable, complete,
70	consistent); it helps you say no (Jared Spool, "Creating Great Design
71	Principles"); it is not fluff and not a goal in disguise (Richard
72	Rumelt, *Good Strategy/Bad Strategy*); it is not permission-to-play —
73	something every competent product already does (Patrick Lencioni, "Make
74	Your Values Mean Something"); and it implies at least one practice and
75	at least one check.
76	
77	## The principles
78	
79	### Consistent, not uniform (`consistent-not-uniform`)
80	
81	**Statement.**
82	- Every interaction type MUST name the product's things and actions with
83	  the product's one vocabulary, as the experience guidance corpus
84	  records it.
85	- Every interaction type MUST follow, for its form and idiom, the
86	  platform interface guidelines the corpus names for that type.
87	- Where a platform guideline names an action differently from the
88	  vocabulary, the platform's word MUST be used in that interaction
89	  type and the mapping recorded in the vocabulary.
90	- A rule of the corpus MAY be varied for one interaction type only
91	  with the variation and its reason recorded in the corpus.
92	
93	**Rationale.** A product reached through a command line, a web page,
94	and a chat window is three products when each names the same object
95	differently, and a foreign one when its command line ignores the
96	terminal's conventions to imitate its web page. People carry their
97	expectations from the platform they are on — Nielsen Norman Group's
98	usability heuristic "consistency and standards" and Jakob's law of
99	internet user experience — and from the last place they met the
100	product. The GOV.UK design principles put it as "be consistent, not
101	uniform": the same language and patterns wherever possible, without a
102	straitjacket. Words and rules are shared; form follows the platform.
103	
104	**Implications.**
105	- The product designer role maintains the vocabulary, its per-platform
106	  mappings, and the named platform guidelines per interaction type in
107	  the corpus.
108	- The product designer role screens every interaction type's text
109	  against the vocabulary.
110	- BC-shops building an interaction cite the platform guideline the
111	  corpus names for its type.
112	- The product designer role records each variation with its reason; an
113	  unrecorded variation is a finding against the corpus.
114	
115	### Core-task parity (`core-task-parity`)
116	
117	**Statement.**
118	- Every interaction type the product offers MUST support every task on
119	  the corpus's core-task list.
120	- An option the product offers in one interaction type MUST be
121	  reachable in every other interaction type that presents the same
122	  task.
123	
124	**Rationale.** A voice assistant that can start an order but only a
125	screen can confirm it strands the person who has no screen; a chat
126	interface that offers three choices only one of which the graphical
127	interface shows teaches people that the product hides things. Google's
128	conversation design guidelines and Amazon's Alexa design guide converge
129	on the rule: voice-first but not voice-only, every option offered in
130	one modality reachable in the other, the core message the same across
131	them. Parity of tasks and options is what lets a person move between
132	interaction types without relearning what the product can do.
133	
134	**Implications.**
135	- The product designer role keeps the core-task list in the corpus.
136	- The product designer role screens each new interaction type against
137	  the list before delivery.
138	- BC-shops that add an option to one interaction type add it to every
139	  other type presenting that task.
140	- The PO role's acceptance scenarios for a task name the interaction
141	  types it must hold on.
142	
143	### The agent is a user (`agent-is-a-user`)
144	
145	**Statement.**
146	- Every interface an agent uses to reach the product — a tool
147	  definition, a command line, an API, or an SDK (a closed set) — MUST
148	  be designed as an interface: named for its caller, its behavior
149	  stated in its documentation, and screened by the product designer
150	  role.
151	- An agent-facing interface MUST NOT expose a capability a person could
152	  not reach through some interaction type.
153	
154	**Rationale.** A tool whose parameters are named for the implementer
155	rather than the caller is misread by the agent calling it, and the
156	agent's failure is recorded as the agent's. Nielsen Norman Group's "AI
157	Agents as Users" states the shift plainly — "user" is no longer
158	synonymous with "human" — and Anthropic's guidance on building agents
159	asks for as much care in the agent-computer interface as in the human
160	one. This principle is `actor-neutral-discipline` applied at the
161	interface: the discipline of design does not lapse because the user is
162	an agent, and an agent gains no capability a person lacks. An interface
163	no one designed is still an interface; it is only an undesigned one.
164	
165	**Implications.**
166	- The solutions architect role submits contracts, command lines, and
167	  tool definitions to the product designer role's screen before they
168	  are published.
169	- BC-shops write tool and API documentation for the caller, with the
170	  same care as user-facing help.
171	- The product designer role screens agent-facing interfaces against
172	  the corpus with the same patterns as human-facing ones.
173	
174	### Evidence, not opinion (`evidence-not-opinion`)
175	
176	**Statement.**
177	- A claim that an interaction is usable MUST rest on observed use — a
178	  user test, a tested prototype, or measured task completion (a closed
179	  set the corpus may extend) — or be labeled a hypothesis.

# Experience principles

## What this set governs

This is the experience-scope principle set: the standing rules for how
the product's interactions are designed, whichever interaction type a
person or an agent reaches the product by — command line, terminal,
graphical or web, API and SDK, conversational, voice, or a generated
document. It is a peer of the working-scope set,
[Founding principles](principles.md), which governs how every activity
is performed, and of the architecture-scope set,
[Architecture principles](architecture-principles.md), which governs
what the designed system must look like; this set governs what a person
or an agent meets when they use it. It is the first layer of the
experience guidance corpus the
[product designer role](roles/lead-product-designer.md) owns; the
guidelines that apply it to each interaction type sit beneath it.
Backticked slugs cite principles; a slug not defined in this document is
defined in the working or architecture set. The terms interaction type,
experience guidance corpus, generated interface, BC-shop, contract, and
intent are defined in the [glossary](glossary.md). Two words carry one
sense each here: an *agent* is a software caller using the product on
someone's behalf; an *assistant interaction* is one in which the
product itself acts on an intent the person stated rather than on a
command — conversational, voice, or an assistant acting for the person
(a closed set; the solutions architect role is the lead shop's
architecture role). Where a principle here applies another set's
principle at the experience level, the frontmatter declares the lineage
in `derives-from` instead of restating the rule as a second authority.

## What a good principle looks like

This section restates the shared definition from the
[principle-set typedef](artifacts/principle-set.md) so this document can
be read alone; the restatement is a rendering, not a second authority.

A principle is a standing rule, in four parts: a name, a statement, a
rationale, and implications.

- The **statement** is the rule. It carries the only normative keywords
  (MUST, SHOULD, MAY — interpreted per BCP 14 when, and only when, they
  appear in capitals) and is testable: shown a piece of work, you can
  answer yes or no. A statement carrying more than one obligation
  presents one obligation per bullet.
- The **rationale** says why the rule earns its place: the failure it
  prevents, shown as a generic example; well-known external references
  may support it, the product's own history never appears. Rationales
  stay prose.
- The **implications** are the price tag: one implication per bullet,
  the concrete change each named actor absorbs to honor the rule. They
  add no obligations — every implication must be derivable from the
  statement.

A good principle passes the tests applied in the fitness screen at the
end: its statement is testable (TOGAF's understandable, complete,
consistent); it helps you say no (Jared Spool, "Creating Great Design
Principles"); it is not fluff and not a goal in disguise (Richard
Rumelt, *Good Strategy/Bad Strategy*); it is not permission-to-play —
something every competent product already does (Patrick Lencioni, "Make
Your Values Mean Something"); and it implies at least one practice and
at least one check.

## The principles

### Consistent, not uniform (`consistent-not-uniform`)

**Statement.**
- Every interaction type MUST name the product's things and actions with
  the product's one vocabulary, as the experience guidance corpus
  records it.
- Every interaction type MUST follow, for its form and idiom, the
  platform interface guidelines the corpus names for that type.
- Where a platform guideline names an action differently from the
  vocabulary, the platform's word MUST be used in that interaction
  type and the mapping recorded in the vocabulary.
- A rule of the corpus MAY be varied for one interaction type only
  with the variation and its reason recorded in the corpus.

**Rationale.** A product reached through a command line, a web page,
and a chat window is three products when each names the same object
differently, and a foreign one when its command line ignores the
terminal's conventions to imitate its web page. People carry their
expectations from the platform they are on — Nielsen Norman Group's
usability heuristic "consistency and standards" and Jakob's law of
internet user experience — and from the last place they met the
product. The GOV.UK design principles put it as "be consistent, not
uniform": the same language and patterns wherever possible, without a
straitjacket. Words and rules are shared; form follows the platform.

**Implications.**
- The product designer role maintains the vocabulary, its per-platform
  mappings, and the named platform guidelines per interaction type in
  the corpus.
- The product designer role screens every interaction type's text
  against the vocabulary.
- BC-shops building an interaction cite the platform guideline the
  corpus names for its type.
- The product designer role records each variation with its reason; an
  unrecorded variation is a finding against the corpus.

### Core-task parity (`core-task-parity`)

**Statement.**
- Every interaction type the product offers MUST support every task on
  the corpus's core-task list.
- An option the product offers in one interaction type MUST be
  reachable in every other interaction type that presents the same
  task.

**Rationale.** A voice assistant that can start an order but only a
screen can confirm it strands the person who has no screen; a chat
interface that offers three choices only one of which the graphical
interface shows teaches people that the product hides things. Google's
conversation design guidelines and Amazon's Alexa design guide converge
on the rule: voice-first but not voice-only, every option offered in
one modality reachable in the other, the core message the same across
them. Parity of tasks and options is what lets a person move between
interaction types without relearning what the product can do.

**Implications.**
- The product designer role keeps the core-task list in the corpus.
- The product designer role screens each new interaction type against
  the list before delivery.
- BC-shops that add an option to one interaction type add it to every
  other type presenting that task.
- The PO role's acceptance scenarios for a task name the interaction
  types it must hold on.

### The agent is a user (`agent-is-a-user`)

**Statement.**
- Every interface an agent uses to reach the product — a tool
  definition, a command line, an API, or an SDK (a closed set) — MUST
  be designed as an interface: named for its caller, its behavior
  stated in its documentation, and screened by the product designer
  role.
- An agent-facing interface MUST NOT expose a capability a person could
  not reach through some interaction type.

**Rationale.** A tool whose parameters are named for the implementer
rather than the caller is misread by the agent calling it, and the
agent's failure is recorded as the agent's. Nielsen Norman Group's "AI
Agents as Users" states the shift plainly — "user" is no longer
synonymous with "human" — and Anthropic's guidance on building agents
asks for as much care in the agent-computer interface as in the human
one. This principle is `actor-neutral-discipline` applied at the
interface: the discipline of design does not lapse because the user is
an agent, and an agent gains no capability a person lacks. An interface
no one designed is still an interface; it is only an undesigned one.

**Implications.**
- The solutions architect role submits contracts, command lines, and
  tool definitions to the product designer role's screen before they
  are published.
- BC-shops write tool and API documentation for the caller, with the
  same care as user-facing help.
- The product designer role screens agent-facing interfaces against
  the corpus with the same patterns as human-facing ones.

### Evidence, not opinion (`evidence-not-opinion`)

  user test, a tested prototype, or measured task completion (a closed

  decision in the corpus, and labels the rest hypotheses.
- The PM role treats a wireframe or sketch from any role as input to be

- BC-shops label an untested interaction's usability a hypothesis when
  they deliver it.

### Accessible by standard (`accessible-by-standard`)

- Every non-web interaction — command line, terminal, voice, and
  assistant interactions (a closed set; APIs and SDKs are agent-facing

**Implications.**

- BC-shops test each interaction with assistive technology before
  delivery and attach the result.
- The PO role's acceptance scenarios for an interaction include its
  accessibility criteria.

### Errors guide recovery (`errors-guide-recovery`)

**Statement.**

  person can do next.
- An error MUST NOT expose an internal identifier or message in place

- The solutions architect role's contracts define error responses that

### Control stays with the person (`control-stays-with-the-person`)

**Statement.**

  action the corpus classes as hard to reverse.

12	# Glossary
13	
14	## How the list combines
15	
16	The defined-term list is this glossary combined with every schema element
17	name. Per the `use-defined-terms` principle, a writer choosing between
18	terms uses one of these when one fits.
19	
20	## Terms
21	
22	- **artifact type** — a named, schema-defined document type (e.g.
23	  `decision-brief`); the term the schema registry uses. Not "kind".
24	- **data type** — a named, schema-defined structure that is not a
25	  human-readable document (e.g. `review`); passed between process steps.
26	- **simple type** — a JSON Schema primitive (`string`, `integer`,
27	  `boolean`, `array`, `object`), usable inline without registration.
28	- **typedef** — the single source a type is generated from; templates and
29	  schema fragments are its renderings (owned by shopsystem-knowledge).
30	- **schema** — the machine-checkable shape of a type: fields, types,
31	  enums, required sections.
32	- **process definition** — the source of truth for a process: header
33	  (purpose, outcomes, roles), data section, steps section.
34	- **step** — one unit of a process: an agent step (carries a prompt) or a
35	  runtime step (carries `set`, `run`, or `branches`; no prose).
36	- **rendering** — a generated output of a definition (a skill, a
37	  diagram, a template); never edited by hand, never the source of truth.
38	- **guiding statement** — an optional header element of a process
39	  definition that directs judgment across the whole process; compiled
40	  into every rendering.
41	- **fitness set** — judged (never executed) Given/When/Then scenarios
42	  scoring an artifact type's quality.
43	- **guideline** — prose quality rules for an artifact type, each with a
44	  test, a criterion, and a yes/no decision.
45	- **role** — a named capability contract and set of accountabilities,
46	  assigned by process steps to whoever fills it; sequencing lives in
47	  process definitions, not roles.
48	- **principle** — a standing rule about how we work: name, statement,
49	  rationale, implications (see the principles document's opening
50	  definition).
51	- **seed layer** — the hand-approved definitions the regress terminates
52	  at: the principle set plus one typedef per definition document type.
53	- **owner** — the role that approves changes to a definition; named in
54	  every definition's frontmatter.
55	- **definition chain** — the six linked definitions of good for one
56	  artifact type; required before instances are authored or rewritten.
57	- **keeper** — a corpus record whose action is keep-rewrite; rewritten
58	  forward through its type's approved chain, never used as-is.
59	- **rewrite-forward** — the default for keepers: re-author to the
60	  approved standard; repair-in-place only for records already at the bar.
61	- **rebaseline** — Phase 1 of the re-founding arc: the active tree comes
62	  to hold only chain-conforming records; retired mass moves to the
63	  archive.
64	- **scope** (of a principle set) — the level the set governs and whose
65	  context it loads into: working (every activity), architecture (the
66	  designed system), or experience (the product's interactions).
67	- **transcript** — the runtime log of turns; unscoped, not a governed
68	  artifact, never loaded into context.
69	- **conversation** — a scoped, bounded discussion attached to exactly one
70	  anchor; every conversation belongs to a process.
71	- **anchor** — the governed record a conversation attaches to: a session
72	  record, a review record, or a work item; carries the conversation's
73	  state across transcript boundaries.
74	- **conversation type** — discovery (anchor: a session record), review
75	  (anchor: a review record and its outcomes), or work (anchor: a work
76	  item).
77	- **session record** — the anchor record of a discovery conversation:
78	  outcome, produced and revised lists, open threads, select quotes.
79	- **review** — one bounded conversation in which the authority decides
80	  on presented material. Replaces "sitting".
81	- **review record** — the anchor record of a review: the material
82	  presented and the outcomes applied; each decision traces in the
83	  changed artifacts' Document History, never in a standing ledger.
84	- **park** — the failsafe for work that cannot pass review within its
85	  round cap: set aside with a filed finding.
86	- **round cap** — the declared maximum review rounds before a loop's
87	  failsafe exit fires.
88	- **action** — the approved choice for one record: keep-rewrite, keep,
89	  retire, or terminal, with its target.
90	- **authority-call** — a row marker on a migration-plan row awaiting a
91	  decision from the authority; not an action — the row has no effect and
92	  is out of scope for any run until ruled.
93	- **action table** — the table of records and their actions; approved row
94	  by row or in blocks at a review. Drives any bulk record change.
95	- **close-out** — the mechanical execution of the migration plan's
96	  pre-decided retire and terminal actions: snapshot, delete, archive
97	  move, a loud post-check, and the branch promotion; no review loop.
98	  All stages run consecutively at cut-over.
99	- **snapshot tag** — the annotated git tag (`pre-migration`) on `main`'s
100	  pre-execution commit, preserving the full corpus for terminal-recovery;
101	  after close-out a terminal record exists only there.
102	- **migration plan** — the rebaseline's action table plus the order of
103	  the per-type migration runs. Replaces "rebaseline bill".
104	- **run** — one execution of a process, anchored to a work item; states:
105	  running, held, done, cancelled.
106	- **hold** — a run state: paused with its step and data preserved in its
107	  anchor, by inactivity or by an ask; a held run is resumed or
108	  cancelled, never dropped.
109	- **checkpoint** — updating a conversation's anchor when a transcript
110	  ends mid-conversation; a checkpoint is not a close.
111	- **branched conversation** — a conversation run as a sub-process of
112	  another run; its anchor records the parent (`branched-from`).
113	- **Bounded Context** — a deliberately drawn region of the product with
114	  one internal language, one model, and one set of contracts to other
115	  regions; drawn by design, never discovered after the fact (Evans,
116	  *Domain-Driven Design*).
117	- **shop** — the entity that builds, operates, and evolves part of the
118	  product. Two types: the lead shop (the system-level coordinator; owns
119	  product-level artifacts and no Bounded Context) and the BC-shop (owns
120	  and produces exactly one Bounded Context).
121	- **activity** — a discrete unit of work performed inside a shop,
122	  following a contract or process, with inputs, outcomes, and provenance
123	  recorded. What an actor is stays unconstrained; the activity has the
124	  same shape whoever performs it.
125	- **contract** — a named, versioned statement of what one entity
126	  promises another: the schemas exchanged, the meaning of each
127	  operation, the error behavior, and the relationship kind. Offered as a
128	  product contract (on a Bounded Context) or an operational contract (on
129	  a shop); nothing outside a contract is promised.
130	- **relationship kind** — the named pattern a contract declares for how
131	  two Bounded Contexts relate, drawn from the context-mapping catalogue
132	  (Evans, *Domain-Driven Design*): customer–supplier, conformist,
133	  anti-corruption layer, open host service, published language, shared
134	  kernel, or separate ways.
135	- **vehicle** — the message type a request to a Bounded Context shop
136	  travels in; chosen from the pre-state, never from the request's
137	  wording.
138	- **pre-state** — what a Bounded Context actually is before a change,
139	  read from its contracts and its scenario register, never from its
140	  internals.
141	- **framing** — the PM role's recorded statement of what a request is
142	  about: the originator, the problem taken to be worth solving, and the
143	  outcome it serves; the exclusive decision of `lead-pm`.
144	- **acceptance scenario** — a Gherkin scenario that states, as a
145	  requirement, what counts as done for one behavior; co-produced by the
146	  PO role and the owning Bounded Context shop; held in that shop's
147	  scenario register.
148	- **scenario register** — a Bounded Context shop's own list of the
149	  acceptance scenarios it holds, with their hashes and states; read in
150	  full across every context when a claim spans contexts.
151	- **ask** — a question one activity puts to another role in place of
152	  its output, carrying a default and a checkpoint; the run holds, the
153	  role answers, the step resumes — never a wait in place (data type
154	  `ask`; process-definition typedef §Run lifecycle).
155	- **clarify** — an ask from a Bounded Context shop to the lead shop on
156	  scope, vocabulary, structure, or contract; answered by the role whose
157	  domain the question falls in.
158	- **decomposition** — the solutions architect's record of which Bounded
159	  Context owns which capability, and the relationship kind of each
160	  contract between contexts.
161	- **enabler work** — technical work that makes a feature possible;
162	  recommended by the solutions architect, placed in the backlog by the
163	  PO role.
164	- **interaction type** — one way a person or an agent reaches the
165	  product: command line (CLI), full-screen terminal (TUI), graphical or
166	  web (GUI), API and SDK, conversational, voice, or a generated document
167	  or notification; each honours its own conventions within one
168	  experience. The experience guidelines cover conversational and voice
169	  together as the `assistant` guideline.
170	- **experience guidance corpus** — the product designer role's
171	  principle set and guidelines for the experience: design principles,
172	  vocabulary and voice, core-task parity across interaction types,
173	  interaction patterns per type, and the accessibility target; the
174	  role's exclusive domain.
175	- **originator** — whoever expresses intent at the product's edge: a
176	  person, a shop, or a system outside the product.
177	- **generated interface** — an interface whose form the product composes
178	  at run time from the person's context, within constraints the
179	  experience guidance corpus states; a form, not an interaction type.
180	- **assistant interaction** — an interaction in which the product acts on
181	  an intent the person stated rather than on a command — conversational,
182	  voice, or an assistant acting for the person (a closed set); the locus
183	  of control is the product's, so the experience principles bound it.
184	- **intent** — a desired outcome expressed by an originator at the
185	  product's edge; enters the product through a contract and keeps its
186	  provenance through every translation and delegation.
187	
188	## Document History
189	
190	| Version | Date | Kind | Entry |
191	|---|---|---|---|

  artifact type; required before instances are authored or rewritten.
- **keeper** — a corpus record whose action is keep-rewrite; rewritten
  forward through its type's approved chain, never used as-is.
- **rewrite-forward** — the default for keepers: re-author to the
  approved standard; repair-in-place only for records already at the bar.
- **rebaseline** — Phase 1 of the re-founding arc: the active tree comes
  to hold only chain-conforming records; retired mass moves to the
  archive.
- **scope** (of a principle set) — the level the set governs and whose
  context it loads into: working (every activity), architecture (the
  designed system), or experience (the product's interactions).
- **transcript** — the runtime log of turns; unscoped, not a governed
  artifact, never loaded into context.
- **conversation** — a scoped, bounded discussion attached to exactly one
  anchor; every conversation belongs to a process.
- **anchor** — the governed record a conversation attaches to: a session
  record, a review record, or a work item; carries the conversation's
  state across transcript boundaries.
- **conversation type** — discovery (anchor: a session record), review
  (anchor: a review record and its outcomes), or work (anchor: a work
  item).
- **session record** — the anchor record of a discovery conversation:
  outcome, produced and revised lists, open threads, select quotes.
- **review** — one bounded conversation in which the authority decides
  on presented material. Replaces "sitting".
- **review record** — the anchor record of a review: the material
  presented and the outcomes applied; each decision traces in the
  changed artifacts' Document History, never in a standing ledger.
- **park** — the failsafe for work that cannot pass review within its
  round cap: set aside with a filed finding.
- **round cap** — the declared maximum review rounds before a loop's
  failsafe exit fires.
- **action** — the approved choice for one record: keep-rewrite, keep,
  retire, or terminal, with its target.
- **authority-call** — a row marker on a migration-plan row awaiting a
  decision from the authority; not an action — the row has no effect and
  is out of scope for any run until ruled.
- **action table** — the table of records and their actions; approved row
  by row or in blocks at a review. Drives any bulk record change.
- **close-out** — the mechanical execution of the migration plan's
  pre-decided retire and terminal actions: snapshot, delete, archive
  move, a loud post-check, and the branch promotion; no review loop.
  All stages run consecutively at cut-over.
- **snapshot tag** — the annotated git tag (`pre-migration`) on `main`'s
  pre-execution commit, preserving the full corpus for terminal-recovery;
  after close-out a terminal record exists only there.
- **migration plan** — the rebaseline's action table plus the order of
  the per-type migration runs. Replaces "rebaseline bill".
- **run** — one execution of a process, anchored to a work item; states:
  running, held, done, cancelled.
- **hold** — a run state: paused with its step and data preserved in its
  anchor, by inactivity or by an ask; a held run is resumed or
  cancelled, never dropped.
- **checkpoint** — updating a conversation's anchor when a transcript
  ends mid-conversation; a checkpoint is not a close.
- **branched conversation** — a conversation run as a sub-process of
  another run; its anchor records the parent (`branched-from`).
- **Bounded Context** — a deliberately drawn region of the product with
  one internal language, one model, and one set of contracts to other
  regions; drawn by design, never discovered after the fact (Evans,
  *Domain-Driven Design*).
- **shop** — the entity that builds, operates, and evolves part of the
  product. Two types: the lead shop (the system-level coordinator; owns
  product-level artifacts and no Bounded Context) and the BC-shop (owns
  and produces exactly one Bounded Context).
- **activity** — a discrete unit of work performed inside a shop,
  following a contract or process, with inputs, outcomes, and provenance
  recorded. What an actor is stays unconstrained; the activity has the
  same shape whoever performs it.
- **contract** — a named, versioned statement of what one entity
  promises another: the schemas exchanged, the meaning of each
  operation, the error behavior, and the relationship kind. Offered as a
  product contract (on a Bounded Context) or an operational contract (on
  a shop); nothing outside a contract is promised.
- **relationship kind** — the named pattern a contract declares for how
  two Bounded Contexts relate, drawn from the context-mapping catalogue
  (Evans, *Domain-Driven Design*): customer–supplier, conformist,
  anti-corruption layer, open host service, published language, shared
  kernel, or separate ways.
- **vehicle** — the message type a request to a Bounded Context shop
  travels in; chosen from the pre-state, never from the request's
  wording.
- **pre-state** — what a Bounded Context actually is before a change,
  read from its contracts and its scenario register, never from its
  internals.
- **framing** — the PM role's recorded statement of what a request is
  about: the originator, the problem taken to be worth solving, and the
  outcome it serves; the exclusive decision of `lead-pm`.
- **acceptance scenario** — a Gherkin scenario that states, as a
  requirement, what counts as done for one behavior; co-produced by the
  PO role and the owning Bounded Context shop; held in that shop's
  scenario register.
- **scenario register** — a Bounded Context shop's own list of the
  acceptance scenarios it holds, with their hashes and states; read in
  full across every context when a claim spans contexts.
- **ask** — a question one activity puts to another role in place of
  its output, carrying a default and a checkpoint; the run holds, the
  role answers, the step resumes — never a wait in place (data type
  `ask`; process-definition typedef §Run lifecycle).
- **clarify** — an ask from a Bounded Context shop to the lead shop on
  scope, vocabulary, structure, or contract; answered by the role whose
  domain the question falls in.
- **decomposition** — the solutions architect's record of which Bounded
  Context owns which capability, and the relationship kind of each
  contract between contexts.
- **enabler work** — technical work that makes a feature possible;
  recommended by the solutions architect, placed in the backlog by the
  PO role.
- **interaction type** — one way a person or an agent reaches the
  product: command line (CLI), full-screen terminal (TUI), graphical or
  web (GUI), API and SDK, conversational, voice, or a generated document
  or notification; each honours its own conventions within one
  experience. The experience guidelines cover conversational and voice
  together as the `assistant` guideline.
- **experience guidance corpus** — the product designer role's
  principle set and guidelines for the experience: design principles,
  vocabulary and voice, core-task parity across interaction types,
  interaction patterns per type, and the accessibility target; the
  role's exclusive domain.
- **originator** — whoever expresses intent at the product's edge: a
  person, a shop, or a system outside the product.
- **generated interface** — an interface whose form the product composes
  at run time from the person's context, within constraints the
  experience guidance corpus states; a form, not an interaction type.
- **assistant interaction** — an interaction in which the product acts on
  an intent the person stated rather than on a command — conversational,
  voice, or an assistant acting for the person (a closed set); the locus
  of control is the product's, so the experience principles bound it.
- **intent** — a desired outcome expressed by an originator at the
  product's edge; enters the product through a contract and keeps its
  provenance through every translation and delegation.

within it, on Nielsen Norman Group's four dimensions of tone of voice.
Read by the [assistant guideline](../guidelines/experience-assistant.md)
rule 6, the [document guideline](../guidelines/experience-document.md)
rule 3, and the [interaction fitness set](../fitness/interaction.fitness.md)
scenario 6. An entry means: text in any interaction type is written at
this setting, varied only as the "when it varies" column allows. The
dimensions are NN/g's; every setting is a hypothesis proposed by design
judgment until user research confirms it.

## Entries

| Dimension or trait | Setting | When it varies | Source | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| persona | the product speaks as itself — "I" for the assistant, never presenting as a person | never | assistant guideline rule 6; Google's conversation design guidelines (persona) | hypothesis |
| formal – casual | plain and direct, neither formal nor casual | never | design judgment | hypothesis |
| serious – funny | serious | never | design judgment | hypothesis |
| respectful – irreverent | respectful | never | design judgment | hypothesis |
| matter-of-fact – enthusiastic | matter-of-fact | a completed task may be acknowledged in one clause, never celebrated | design judgment | hypothesis |
| on error (trait) | the same voice, shorter: what happened, the cause, the next step | never | common guideline rule 3 | hypothesis |

## Checks

[Assistant guideline](../guidelines/experience-assistant.md) rule 6;
[document guideline](../guidelines/experience-document.md) rule 3;
[interaction fitness set](../fitness/interaction.fitness.md) scenario
6.

## Document History

| Version | Date | Kind | Entry |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2026-08-26 | update | Seeded on NN/g's four tone dimensions. |
| 1 | 2026-08-26 | review | Screened: findings — settings sourced to the base writing style, which carries no tone position, and to NN/g, which defines the axis not the setting; the error trait reversed rule 3's order. |
| 2 | 2026-08-26 | update | Repairs: settings sourced as design judgment and marked hypothesis; the error trait follows rule 3's order. |
